summary: Project Bits is an interactive game where players create and manage their own space missions. Players must make engineering decisions to complete each mission successfully.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?“Bits” is an interactive video game inspired by the movie Pixels that teaches space engineering. It works through missions that players solve using theoretical NASA data, controlling a character animated frame-by-frame with actions and abilities scripted in Godot.

What benefits does it have? It makes learning space engineering accessible and interactive, sparks a passion for discovery, and encourages awareness of one's environment and the Sustainable Development Goals.

What is the intended impact of the project? To encourage passionate young people to take an interest in the place where they live and promote the integration of the Sustainable Development Goals into their daily lives.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? To bring “Bits” to life, we combined several tools focused on game development:

  • Game Engine & Language: We chose Godot for its ease of use and intuitiveness in building features and animations, coding the character's actions and abilities in its built-in language, GDScript.
  • Artificial Intelligence: We used Claude Code to develop character movement in the “prologue” act scenes faster and more efficiently, alongside Gemini.
  • Hosting, Data & Workflow: We hosted the game on itch.io and utilized Supabase, GitHub, Google Docs, and NASA databases.
  • Hardware & Materials: Computers and paper, driven by a passionate team.
How is your project creative? It adapts to the team's varied interests in pursuit of continuous improvement and delivers interactive gameplay that sparks a passion for discovery. On the development side, we crafted the character's movement animations by designing frames from multiple photos of the same character inside Godot, resulting in visually appealing character and world designs.

What factors did your team consider? We prioritized ease of use and intuitiveness for both the player and the development workflow (which guided our choice of Godot), alongside user experience, design, and visual appeal.

How are resources (mass, power, budget) managed?

BITS does not use mass, power, or budget as resources that the player spends. Instead, they are concepts learned through real NASA data:

  • Power: This is the theme of the planet Yuki, which lost its electricity. Andrew solves it through missions about deployable solar panels (ChargerSat-1), UL-certified batteries, and inhibits. On Zero, Bels has to collect 3 solar panels.
  • Mass: Appears in questions and risks, such as the maximum mass of a 3U CubeSat (4 kg) or the "mass out of tolerance" risk.
  • Budget: Appears in cost-related questions: NASA pays up to $300,000 USD for launches through CSLI, it is recommended to reserve at least 10% for contingencies, and LightSail-2 raised over $1.24 million USD via crowdfunding.
  • The only thing spent in the game is suit health (100 points). If it runs out—or if time expires—the planet resets and the player can try again as many times as they want. There are no credits or scores.

How does the launch work?

  • Start: The "Earth – Launch Day" scene shows the five friends boarding the rocket, the countdown, and liftoff. Then, a "module separation failure" alert triggers, and each module lands on a different planet. This is based on a real-world risk: premature deployment, which is prevented using two burn wires.
  • Between planets: Before taking off, the player completes a 3-step checklist. First, they dock the rescued friend's module, and then they apply two lessons learned on that planet, such as installing the second burn wire or removing the "Remove Before Flight" pin. Each trip uses an orbit type designed by NASA Goddard's Mission Design Lab (MDL): geostationary, lunar, libration, deep space, and controlled deorbit to return to Earth.
  • Ending: The rebuilt spacecraft deploys real climate CubeSats (IceCube, MinXSS), linked to the Sustainable Development Goals.
  • Real-world rules in missions: Waiting 45 minutes before transmitting, "the rocket doesn't wait for the CubeSats," and "it's cheaper to build two satellites at the same time."

Is there a co-op mode?

No. BITS is a single-player game. Teamwork is built into the story: the player controls the five friends one by one, one on each planet. Each character has an ability tied to an engineering discipline (power, propulsion and attitude control, thermal, communications, and risk & redundancy), and the ship is only completed when all five modules are brought together. Rayan's holographic clone is a character ability, not a second player. There is no local or online multiplayer.

How is the database used?

At startup, the game reads preguntas_juego and riesgos from Supabase using a read-only public key (RLS). In each playthrough, it randomly selects a question or risk matching each mission's topic, so they change from one run to the next. The incorrect options for risks are pulled from the solutions of other risks. Each mission displays its source, such as "Supabase: riesgos #13." If there is no internet connection, the game falls back on a local copy of the data. In English, it uses translations stored directly inside the game.
